title: Rabbi Joshua Keeps the People's Day
hookLine: a sage keeps Yom Kippur on the court's day, not his own
carry: the holy days belong to the whole people
tomorrow: can a whole way of life fit in one sentence?

lines: WHO DECIDES WHICH DAY IS HOLY?
cards: Noa's college calendar arrived: move-in, midterms, finals. She laid it next to the Jewish calendar and groaned. Yom Kippur lands on her first chemistry quiz.
Couldn't she just keep it a day later, on her own? Who decides which day is holy? The Mishnah tells of a great sage who had to answer that the hard way.

teach.b: The Torah calls the festivals mo'adim, appointed seasons, "which ye shall proclaim in their appointed season." Proclaim.

In those days the court declared each new month when witnesses saw the new moon, and the festivals followed. One year, Rabbi Joshua was sure the court's head, Rabban Gamliel, had accepted the wrong witnesses.

By his own count, Yom Kippur fell on a different day. So Rabban Gamliel ordered him: come to me with your staff and your money on the day you count as Yom Kippur. Things you'd never carry on the holiest day.
Rabbi Akiva found him troubled and comforted him with the verse: which you shall proclaim. The days are the ones the court proclaims.

teach.h: COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.
teach.b: So Rabbi Joshua took his staff and his money and walked.
And Rabban Gamliel stood, kissed him on the head, and said: come in peace, my teacher and my student. Here's the teaching. Jewish holy days aren't a private schedule.
They're appointed for the whole people together. Today the Hebrew calendar is worked out in advance, so Jews everywhere fast on the same Yom Kippur.

Your year is your share of that one calendar, kept even when a quiz lands on it. Something to tell a friend tonight: a sage carried his wallet on his own Yom Kippur so the people would keep one day together.

how: The Jewish year runs on the Hebrew calendar, once set month by month by a court and now calculated in advance, so Jews everywhere keep the same festival days; students and workers ask for time off ahead, or find a seder, a sukkah or a break-fast near where they are.

o: the vacation days your job gives you
a calendar each family sets for itself
the festivals you keep, your share of the people's calendar

p: came with staff and money on his own Yom Kippur

s: the Torah calls its festivals appointed seasons
Leviticus 23: mo'adim, proclaimed in their appointed season.
in the Mishnah, Rabbi Joshua kept Yom Kippur on his own date anyway
he came to Rabban Gamliel with staff and money on that day, keeping the court's calendar.
Jews in different countries fast on different days for Yom Kippur
the calendar is worked out in advance, so it's the same day everywhere.

games.q: you've moved to a new city for work. Pesach falls midweek, and a friend suggests holding your seder the next weekend instead, when you're both free. what fits Rabbi Joshua's story?
o: keep the seder on its night, and find one to join or host a small one.
move it to the weekend; the date is just a suggestion.
skip it this year; without family it doesn't count.
games.why: the mo'adim are proclaimed for the whole people. Rabbi Joshua kept the court's day, not his own; the seder belongs on the night the people keep it.

practice: Open a calendar and find this year's Yom Kippur, or the next festival. Mark it the way you'd mark something you can't move.
Then name the people keeping that same day with you, near or far, and the one thing you'll do now so you can keep it with them.

wordCard.voice: Your year: the festivals you keep, appointed seasons proclaimed for the whole people, kept in your real life.

orig.note: Hebrew: appointed seasons, the Torah's name for the festivals (Leviticus 23).

carryVoice: Here's the line: the holy days belong to the whole people, and your year is your share. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: which ye shall proclaim in their appointed season
